title: National Petroleum Refiners Association v. Federal Trade Commission
lead: A gasoline-pump disclosure rule tests whether the FTC can establish substantive standards before bringing individual enforcement cases.

actors.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
actors.role: Agency adopting an octane-disclosure trade regulation rule.

actors.name: National Petroleum Refiners Association, another association, and thirty-four refiners
actors.role: Challengers to the rule and the Commission’s authority.

proceedings: The district court held that the FTC lacked substantive rulemaking authority and did not reach remaining challenges.
The D.C. Circuit reversed on June 27, 1973, and remanded those challenges.
limits: This is the 1973 authority holding, not final validation of the octane rule or certification of present FTC powers. The court did not impose liability or a penalty on an individual refiner.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Commission requires an octane rating at covered pumps
sections.cue: What activity did the rule define as unlawful?
paragraphs: The Federal Trade Commission adopted a rule treating failure to display octane ratings as an unfair method of competition and an unfair or deceptive act or practice. It covered refiners or distributors selling to retailers when they owned or leased the pumps through which consumers bought motor gasoline. The required minimum-octane disclosure had to be clear, conspicuous, and permanent, using the specified rating method. The rule allowed legally practical compliance with existing leases and excluded aviation fuel.

Two trade associations and thirty-four refining companies challenged it on statutory, constitutional, procedural, evidentiary, and arbitrary-and-capricious grounds. The district court decided only that the Commission lacked power to make substantive rules. The agency appealed to the D.C. Circuit; no individual violation, damages, or civil penalty was before it.

sources.pinpoint: Facts and procedural posture; opening discussion and nn.1–2

sections.title: The companies read the Act as requiring standards to emerge in individual cases
sections.cue: Which two provisions created the interpretive dispute?
paragraphs: Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act directed prevention of unfair practices through complaints, hearings, findings, and cease-and-desist orders. Section 6(g) authorized rules and regulations to carry out the Act, while neighboring § 6 provisions addressed investigation and reporting. The companies read that context as restricting § 6(g) to procedural and investigatory rules and treated § 5’s express adjudicatory process as exclusive.

History reinforced their position. For decades the Commission had not claimed binding substantive rulemaking, some officials disclaimed it, and later product-labeling and consumer laws expressly granted rulemaking authority. Legislators had described the agency as adjudicatory rather than legislative. Judge J. Skelly Wright, writing with Chief Judge Bazelon and Judge Robinson, addressed these arguments as statutory questions; usefulness alone could not create withheld authority.

sources.pinpoint: Statutory framework; Parts I, IV and VI

sections.title: Wright reads rules as supplementing rather than abolishing adjudication
sections.cue: What would remain to be decided in an enforcement action?
paragraphs: The court found § 6(g)’s language broad enough to include substantive standards. Section 5 prescribed the route to an enforceable order but did not expressly make repeated adjudication the sole way to develop the governing legal rule. Inferring exclusivity assumed that Congress had considered and rejected every supplementary technique.

A rule did not bypass complaint, hearing, findings, a cease-and-desist order, or judicial review against a respondent. For this rule, later adjudication would centrally ask whether the covered pumps displayed ratings; rulemaking could settle the common premise that nondisclosure violated the Act. That binding narrowing distinguished a substantive rule from merely advisory guidance, even though both could induce compliance.

The Supreme Court’s Morton Salt decision supported reading investigatory and enforcement provisions together rather than isolating §§ 5 and 6. Other ancillary-power decisions alone might establish only procedural authority, but analogous decisions supported more. In Storer Broadcasting, a general agency rule narrowed individual hearing issues while preserving an opportunity for waiver. Cases involving communications and power regulators were interpretive analogies, not interchangeable statutory grants.

The companies distinguished the Commission as prosecutorial rather than a licensing or rate-setting regulator. Wright found that adjudicatory control of competition and consumer practices also had major regulatory effects, and the National Labor Relations Board’s similar enforcement structure and rulemaking authority weakened the distinction.

sources.pinpoint: Integrated text; Analogous agency powers; Parts I–III and nn.6–8, 13

sections.title: General proceedings can resolve common questions, but policy is not enough
sections.cue: How did statutory history and long nonuse affect the court’s reading?
paragraphs: Octane disclosure implicated engine needs, buying habits, costs, and alternative disclosure. Rulemaking could collect broader evidence, give advance notice, avoid choosing one firm to bear the first industry-wide obligation, and protect compliant firms from competitors benefiting from enforcement delay. Those advantages supported statutory design; they did not decide whether an agency must always use rulemaking. Discussion of Chenery, Wyman-Gordon, and the circuit’s Bell Aerospace decision did not establish a mandatory-rulemaking rule.

The opinion’s appendix followed the 1914 proposals. An early House bill envisioned a weaker investigatory body and rules tied to limited functions. After President Wilson changed course, the Senate pursued stronger independent enforcement without an express rulemaking provision. Conference combined enforcement and general rulemaking. Neither initial bill alone established the final combination’s meaning.

Statements rejecting legislative powers often distinguished the Interstate Commerce Commission’s immediately operative future-rate orders. These proposed trade rules still required individual enforcement and review. The appendix recognized evidence on both sides rather than treating ambiguous exchanges as unmistakable rejection. Shared concerns about judicial delay, expertise, uncertainty, and inefficient enforcement favored the broader reading with the text.

Nonuse did not forfeit granted power. Earlier disclaimers deserved weight but did not control a legal and historical question within judicial competence. The court independently construed the statute instead of deferring automatically to either agency position. Later specific grants could reflect caution or an effort to end uncertainty. Fair Packaging and Labeling Act history showed a continuing dispute; pending bills indicated study rather than completed legal change.

sources.pinpoint: Practical fairness; Legislative history, nonuse and later statutes; Parts II, IV, VI; appendix; nn.26–40

sections.title: The rulemaking power survives while the rule’s other defects remain open
sections.cue: What safeguards and further proceedings did the judgment preserve?
paragraphs: The recognized authority remained bounded by the Act’s standards and judicial review of procedure, reasons, and scope. Respondents also needed some opportunity to show unusual circumstances warranting waiver, such as a case outside the rule’s rationale or compelling hardship. The court reserved precise waiver procedures and circumstances and granted none to a particular company.

On June 27, 1973, the D.C. Circuit reversed the categorical denial of substantive rulemaking and remanded for the remaining challenges to this rule’s adoption. Rehearing was denied August 6. No separate opinion appeared. The decision neither resolved constitutional and procedural objections nor found the octane evidence sufficient.
